title: These Faraway Planets Are Fluffier Than Cotton Candy!
summary:
Imagine a planet so fluffy it could float in a giant bathtub. That's what astronomers just found! Two planets, called TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, are less dense than cotton candy. They're called "super-puffs."

These planets are huge, about the size of Jupiter. But they're incredibly light. They orbit a star that's like our Sun, but 1,113 light-years away. That's super far!

How did scientists find them? Volunteers were looking at data from a space telescope called TESS. They noticed tiny dips in the star's brightness. Those dips meant planets were passing in front of the star. Cool, right?

To confirm, Dr. George Dransfield and her team used telescopes around the world. One was in Antarctica! The continuous darkness of the Antarctic winter helped them record the longest complete planetary transits ever seen from the ground. Each transit lasted over 11 hours.

The two planets move in a pattern. For every five orbits the inner planet makes, the outer planet makes three. This suggests they formed together from the same disk of gas and dust.

Scientists still don't know how super-puffs form. One idea is that they have big, thick atmospheres of hydrogen and helium around small solid cores. That would make them look huge but stay very light.

Dr. Dransfield hopes to use the James Webb Space Telescope to study their atmospheres. Maybe we'll solve the mystery of these cotton-candy planets soon!
why_it_matters: Learning how planets form — and why some are puffier than cotton candy — helps us understand our own Earth and the solar system, and it shows that even volunteers can help make a space discovery.

background_read: TESS is a NASA space telescope (launched in 2018) that hunts for planets by watching stars for tiny dips in their light.
Scientists found the first 'super-puff' planets around a star called Kepler-51, so fluffy planets are a real puzzle in astronomy.

Antarctica (the icy continent at the bottom of the world) stays dark for months each winter, which helps telescopes there watch the sky for many hours without the Sun getting in the way. The James Webb Space Telescope (the biggest space telescope ever, launched in 2021) can study the air around faraway planets.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers including Dr. George Dransfield, plus volunteers who searched space telescope data
WHAT: Two huge but super-light planets, TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, were found and confirmed
WHERE: They orbit a Sun-like star 1,113 light-years away, and were checked with telescopes around the world, including one in Antarctica
WHY: Scientists want to understand how 'super-puff' planets form, and hope to study their atmospheres with the James Webb Space Telescope

perspectives.description: They love that a planet can be less dense than cotton candy, and that everyday volunteers helped spot something so strange and far away.
They point out that nobody yet knows how super-puffs form, so the discovery is a mystery to solve, not a finished answer.
They would say the long, dark Antarctic winter is what made the record-breaking 11-hour transit measurements possible.
